C1.why: A flat, featureless ribbon at floor value is applied to every wall edge for its entire length, ringing each mass in bright piping so the quadrants read as cut-out cards rather than stone.
C1.q1: Straight up the pale corridor, because it is the only continuously bright surface and the pale piping on both sides tells me exactly where the solid stops.
C1.q2: Coursed brick of varied block sizes in a warm brown, mortar rendered as near-black recessed joints, laid as a flat elevation over the whole solid mass rather than as a wall seen from above.
C1.q3: One rose-coloured horizontal baulk with cream pin-heads at each end near the left wall, a few flat brown vertical posts, and some pale L-brackets — all of them bracing undamaged masonry, so nothing is actually being held.
C1.q4: No — the brick elevation runs to the boundary and terminates in a flat pale ribbon, so there is no cap, no cross-section, and no way to tell the top of a wall from the face of it.
C1.q5: Nothing has happened to it; the stone is intact, the joints are sound, and a few coloured bars have been pinned to walls that show no damage.

C2.why: A four-hundred-year contested line with zero repair hardware in the entire frame answers Q3 with nothing, and it carries C1's pale outline ribbon on top of that.
C2.q1: Up the corridor, for the same reason as C1 — the bright piping outlines the walkable slot unambiguously.
C2.q2: The same coursed brown brick elevation as C1, unbroken and uniform across every quadrant, with black recessed mortar.
C2.q3: Nothing holds them together — the baulk, pins and brackets present in C1 have been removed and what remains is bare masonry with no rope, pin, timber or hide anywhere in frame.
C2.q4: No — identical to C1: elevation to a hairline boundary, then a pale stripe, no top surface.
C2.q5: Nothing has happened here at all; this is new wall, well laid, never touched.

C3.why: The corridor floor is a strict four-tile repeat — measured 0.52 correlation at lag 4 and 0.80 at lag 8 — cycling the same ornamental square panel and the same moss tuft in the same position, so the ground the player walks on is wallpaper.
C3.q1: Up the corridor — the walls read as dark solid mass and the floor as a distinctly paler band, so the walkable slot is unmistakable without any help from an edge marker.
C3.q2: Coursed brick in varied course heights with patches of smaller rubble infill and a red-brown mortar, bounded at every opening by a recessed reveal cut in the wall's own joint colour.
C3.q3: A rose horizontal baulk with cream pin-heads left of the player, flat brown vertical posts lower left and lower right, and pale L-brackets in the upper wall — each a single flat colour with square-cut ends, fixed over sound stone.
C3.q4: No — the reveal at the boundary reads as a shadow gap rather than a cap, so you still cannot distinguish a wall top from a wall face anywhere in the image.
C3.q5: The masonry has been laid and varied by hand and a few braces have been added, but nothing is broken, worn, stained or displaced — it is used-looking wall with no evidence of use.

C4.why: Every brick in every wall-face row carries a highlight band along its top edge and a shadow band along its bottom edge in one identical direction — differencing against C1 isolates a per-block top-bright/bottom-dark emboss that would survive the engine light being switched off.

C5.why: It keeps C3's honest boundary but reverts to the flatter, evenly-coursed wall body, so the masonry loses the hand-laid variation that was the only thing carrying the fiction, and it inherits the same repeating floor.
C5.q1: Up the corridor — same clean dark-mass-versus-pale-band read as C3.
C5.q2: Coursed brick in one dominant course height, far more regular than C3, with the same recessed reveal at the openings.
C5.q3: The same rose baulk with cream pins, flat brown posts and pale L-brackets as C3, in the same places, bracing the same undamaged stone.
C5.q4: No — reveal only, no cap, no cross-section, no top-versus-face distinction.
C5.q5: Less than in C3: the courses are uniform enough that the wall reads as one printed brick sheet stretched over four quadrants.

separator: The top of the list builds its wall boundaries and its damage out of the wall's own material — varied courses, mortar-coloured reveals, hardware set into stone — while the bottom substitutes uniform applied trim, a repeated bevel, or nothing at all, and none of them yet shows a wall that has been broken and then held.
flip_list: Delete the pale edge ribbon in C1, C2 and C4 and rebuild the wall/floor junction the way C3 does it: carry the brick courses right to the edge, then a 2–3px reveal in the same value as the internal mortar, so the boundary is the wall's own joint and not a stripe laid over it.

Break the masonry under every repair element: put a dropped stone, a stepped crack, or a sagging course beneath the rose baulk, each brown post and each L-bracket, so the brace is resisting something instead of decorating sound wall.

Terminate every bar in a real fixing — a driven pin with a countersunk head, a split in the timber radiating from the pin, and a rust bloom running down the stone beneath it — instead of a square-cut end that stops in mid-course.
Drop the cream pin-heads two to three steps below lit-floor value and ring each with a dull darker pixel so they read as struck metal, not as the brightest sparkle in the frame.

Redraw the corridor floor as at least twelve non-symmetric variants and break the cycle: the current strip repeats identically every four tiles and near-identically every eight, which is visible as three matching panels in a single screen.

Cut the square-in-square floor panel or make it a thing — give it a recessed pull on one side, a chipped lip, and a scored arc in the stone where it has been dragged open — because a centred symmetric undamaged frame is ornament in a place where nothing is arranged for anyone's benefit.

Lift the moss out of the floor tile art so it stops repeating on the same grid position every cycle, and desaturate it from chartreuse to a grey-green lichen crust that runs down from damp joints rather than sitting in tile corners.
Give each wall a cap band drawn as the stones seen end-on, with a course rhythm different from the face, so the top of a wall is not the same drawing as its side.

Wear the floor where it is walked: a paler polished track down the traffic line of each corridor, grit and dark accumulation in the joints at the wall bases, so the most-used surface stops being the emptiest one in frame.

Remove the per-brick top-highlight/bottom-shadow emboss from C4's wall-face rows entirely; get relief instead from individual stones sitting proud or sunk relative to their neighbours, which survives any light direction.
